To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

intracellular cytokine detection in peripheral blood lymphocytes by flow cytometry provides a rapid, sensitive and rugged method to characterize changes in the immune system over time in infants and adults.
the production of type 1 and type 2 cytokines in infants and adults are different.
the production of intracellular T‐cell cytokines by infants is different from that of adults and changes over the first year after birth.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of cytokine profiles and the immune response to vaccination in infants.
the development of immune competence in infants and the role of T cell cytokines in the development of the immune system.
the ontogeny of the immune system and the development of immunological memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the immune system is not fully developed at birth and continues to develop during the first year of infancy.
the Th1/Th1 and Th2/Tc1/Tc1 responses of infants are skewed toward Th1 and Tc1, and that the infant Th1 and Th2 cells are less active than adult cells, but Th2 cells become more active with age.
infants have a more immature immune system than adults.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Th1/Th0 and Tc1/T0 ratios in infants are significantly lower than in adults.

the immune system of healthy infants is immature, with Th1 and Tc1 cells lagging behind Th2 and Tc2 cells in development, and that the infant T‐cell cytokine response profile is skewed to Th1 and T‐cell cytotoxicity, but is not polarized to a Th1 or Th2 profile.
infants are less able to mount Th1 and Tc1 cytokine production responses than adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Th1/Th1 and Th2/Th2 cytokine responses of infants are significantly different from adults and that the Th1‐skew is more apparent in infants than in adults, which is in agreement with previous studies.
infants have a lower capacity to produce IFN‐γ and IL‐4 than adults and this is especially true of the helper/inducer T cells.
the immune systems of healthy infants are different from those of adults, and that the Th1 and Th2 systems are skewed in infants compared to those in adults.
